title: Reaching Escape Velocity In Math: The Problem
author: Samantha Lippert
summary: Samantha Lippert uses two videos of one third grader to pose a puzzle: he is automatic with recently learned multiplication facts but still counts on his fingers for subtraction within 10. Borrowing Mark Seidenberg's phonics idea of escape velocity, she argues that strategies are an engine to get students to known facts, not a destination. She traces the gap to curriculum progression being mistaken for learning progression, so fluency was skipped. The cost is a working memory bottleneck that shows up in multi-digit subtraction. Multiplication shows what works: conceptual foundation, small fact sets, daily low-stakes retrieval and homework practice. She ends by promising an intervention to recreate those conditions for subtraction.
points: Strategies such as counting back are essential for building number sense but become a trap when they never fade into recalled facts.
Curriculum progression is not learning progression: moving to the next unit does not mean fact fluency was ever built.
Reconstructing basic facts consumes working memory, which undermines multi-digit subtraction with regrouping and place value.
Automaticity developed quickly in multiplication under explicit sequencing, small fact families, peer quizzing without written strategies and daily retrieval.
The case shows the failure was in instructional conditions, not the child's capacity, so the next step is to recreate those conditions for subtraction.
quotes: Strategies are the engine. Counting back, counting on, making ten, using a known fact.
The goal of a strategy is to get a student to the answer often enough, and efficiently enough, that eventually they don’t need the strategy at all. The fact just becomes known to them.
Too often, curriculum progression is treated as evidence of learning progression.
There was never a deliberate stretch of time spent moving those facts from figuring out to knowing. The fluency was never built for the skill they were learning.
He is simultaneously using working memory to calculate basic facts that other students can retrieve almost instantly.
That tells me this isn’t about whether he can become automatic. It’s about whether his subtraction facts have ever been given the same conditions.
When we keep students in strategies too long, without ever pushing for that shift away from the strategy, they don’t reach that escape velocity. They stay stuck in orbit.
